talks.title: Keynote: BAML - A New Programming Language for Building Agents
talks.teaser: Investigates keynote: BAML - A New Programming Language for Building Agents and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this keynote, speaker Vibb introduces BAML, a domain-specific programming language designed to build reliable, maintainable agentic AI applications. Addressing the common frustration that large language model (LLM) implementations often feel flaky or function only as fragile prototypes, the presentation argues that developers must hold AI to standard software engineering expectations. Unlike cloud infrastructure failures where third-party providers can be blamed, hallucinations and reliability issues fall squarely on the application developer. BAML was created to address this problem by replacing messy string concatenations with type-safe, functional abstractions.

### Key Topics
- **The Reliability Burden in AI Engineering**: In standard software, a 5% failure rate is intolerable. When building AI systems, developers have mistakenly accepted high failure rates, but the responsibility for application correctness rests on the developer rather than LLM providers.
- **Evolution of Developer Tooling**: Just as web development evolved from raw text templates to JSX/TSX in React for static analysis and safety, and data science evolved from plain Python scripts to Jupyter notebooks (`.ipynb`) for rapid iteration loops, AI development needs specialized abstractions rather than string-heavy boilerplate.
- **Problems with String-Based Prompting**: Treating prompts as string templates or chained F-strings makes context engineering brittle, complicates switching models, and introduces slow iteration cycles that discourage finding optimal solutions.
- **BAML Language Design and Features**: BAML models prompts as first-class functions with defined input parameters, return types, and explicit LLM call operators. It features deep editor integration (such as in VS Code) allowing developers to inspect raw rendered prompts, dynamic inputs, raw network requests, model fallbacks, and retry policies.

### Technical Details
- **Function-First Prompts**: Prompts are declared with input parameters and strict return types that support code navigation (e.g., jump-to-definition) and embedded instructions.
- **Testing and Playground**: BAML provides an integrated editor playground where developers can write unit tests, inspect raw prompts versus runtime data, test multimodal inputs (such as images), and instantly observe output parsing.
- **Robust Parsing and Resilience**: BAML parses and cleans up noisy model outputs (such as removing unwanted markdown fences or backtick JSON blocks) and extracts strictly typed structures even when the model includes extra reasoning text or disregards formatting constraints like JSON quotation marks.
- **Model Fallbacks and Retries**: Retry policies—such as exponential backoffs (e.g., waiting 450 ms before retrying GPT-4 mini, then falling back to Sonnet)—are declared and visually inspectable directly within the code.
- **Polyglot and Type Safety**: BAML integrates seamlessly into target codebases, generating native types and client methods for languages like TypeScript and Python. Modifying a BAML schema immediately propagates updated type definitions to the host language.
- **Architecture**: BAML is built in Rust for high execution speed and concurrency, runs completely air-gapped without external dependencies, and works across any LLM.

### Takeaways
BAML aims to bring software engineering rigor—static analysis, type safety, fast feedback loops, and automated parsing—to AI agent development. Started by Vibb and co-founder Aaron at Boundary after growing dissatisfied with complex string-based orchestration frameworks like LangChain, the open-source language is now used in production by over a thousand organizations ranging from Fortune 50 companies and government agencies to small independent developer teams.

talks.title: Docling: Get Your Documents Ready for Gen AI
talks.teaser: Investigates docling: Get Your Documents Ready for Gen AI and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, speakers Michaela and Caesar introduce Docling, an open-source library and SDK maintained by a 15-person team in Zurich, Switzerland, under the Linux Foundation for AI & Data. Docling focuses on converting and parsing complex documents—such as PDFs, Word files, Excel sheets, and CSVs—into a unified, structured representation known as the `dockling document`. The project addresses common failure modes in document ingestion, including broken multi-column layouts and hidden prompt injection instructions, ensuring documents are accurately prepared for generative AI and LLM workflows.

### Key Topics
- **Document Ingestion Challenges & Bad Parsing**: Naive PDF extraction often blends adjacent columns into a single line of text. The speakers highlighted a 1959 scientific paper where separate columns containing the words "vegetative" and "electron microscopy" were merged by parsers into the nonexistent phrase "vegetative electron microscopy," which subsequently poisoned LLM training sets. Furthermore, security and trust issues arise from hidden text, such as white-on-white text containing prompt injections aimed at manipulating automated peer review systems.
- **Unified Architecture & Pipelines**: Docling uses customizable processing pipelines depending on document type:
  - *Basic Pipeline*: Operates without AI to programmatically parse structured files like Word, PowerPoint, and Excel.
  - *Standard PDF Pipeline*: Employs PDF readers combined with layout analysis, reading-order reconstruction, and table structure parsing.
  - *Enrichment Pipeline*: Integrates lightweight classification models (such as an 8 MB model for distinguishing charts, logos, and signatures) and vision-language models (VLMs) for generating contextual picture descriptions.
  - *Small Docling (VLM Pipeline)*: A custom 256-million-parameter vision-language model developed by the team. Small Docling performs layout segmentation, bounding box detection, table reconstruction, and image description in a single shot, and is lightweight enough to run directly on mobile phones.
- **Agentic AI & MCP Integration**: Aligning with the growth of autonomous agents, the team introduced Dockling MCP (Model Context Protocol), enabling AI agents to read, summarize, manipulate, and generate Docling documents. In live demonstrations using LM Studio as an MCP host, Docling parsed remote URLs into markdown, extracted specific page thumbnails, and created structured synthetic documents on the fly.
- **Ecosystem & Deployment**: Beyond Python SDK and CLI access, Docling natively integrates with Langflow for no-code/low-code pipelines, LlamaIndex, Pydantic AI, and Llama Stack. It features `dockling-serve` (a REST API wrapper) and an OpenShift operator developed in collaboration with Red Hat.

### Technical Details
- **Chunking by Structure**: Unlike basic text splitters that cut text strictly by character length, Docling provides specialized chunkers that respect document hierarchy (headers, table cells, lists, and sublists).
- **Doc Tags & Standardization**: Docling uses "doc tags" tokens to capture bounding boxes, reading order, and table headers. The team aims to establish this layout representation as an open industry standard for LLM ingestion.
- **OCR & Layering**: For handwriting and annotations, the standard PDF pipeline provides modular plug-ins allowing users to swap OCR backends, while Small Docling provides native handwriting recognition out of the box. Additionally, auxiliary content such as slide presenter notes can be routed to separate "content layers" so they do not contaminate the primary export.

### Takeaways
Docling provides an open-source, robust document parsing layer essential for high-fidelity generative AI and RAG architectures. By accurately capturing structural context, tables, and multimodal visual elements, it mitigates training-data corruption and prompt-injection risks while offering native integrations for agentic workflows.

talks.title: AI Showdown: Open Source Tools for LLM Face-Offs
talks.teaser: Investigates AI Showdown: Open Source Tools for LLM Face-Offs and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In "AI Showdown: Open Source Tools for LLM Face-Offs," speakers Rishabh Misra and Jigyasa Grover address the critical challenge of selecting large language models (LLMs) for product development amidst rapid model releases. They argue that choosing models based solely on public leaderboards, pricing, or academic benchmarks is flawed because scores rarely reflect real-world user experience, tone, and domain-specific needs. The talk outlines the shift from traditional, objective quantitative machine learning evaluation to modern qualitative and side-by-side LLM assessment, highlighting open-source tooling—particularly Google's LLM Comparator.

### Key Topics
- **Limitations of Traditional Evaluation**: Traditional machine learning relies on objective ground-truth metrics (accuracy, F1, AUC, NDCG) that produce single deterministic scores. In contrast, generative LLM tasks lack a single ground truth, making standard overlap metrics like ROUGE and BERTScore brittle or insufficient for capturing qualities such as helpfulness, safety, and brand loyalty.
- **Open-Source Evaluation Advantage**: Open-source evaluation tools offer transparency, reproducibility, vendor neutrality, and complete audit trails (code, prompts, configs, and outputs), preventing vendor lock-in and meeting regulatory requirements.
- **Google's LLM Comparator**: A Python package developed by Google's People and AI Research (PAIR) team designed for qualitative, side-by-side LLM face-offs combining quantitative scoring with interactive visual analysis.
- **Alternative Tooling Ecosystem**: A comparative breakdown of other tools including EleutherAI's LM Evaluation Harness, OpenAI Evals, Hugging Face Evaluate, and LangChain evaluators.
- **Best Practices and Pitfalls**: Mitigating evaluation biases, calibrating LLM judges, avoiding overall score averaging, and testing specialized capabilities like tool trajectories.

### Technical Details
- **LLM Comparator Workflow**: Installed via `pip`, the library executes an evaluation via its `run_judging_pipeline` function. Users define a prompt set with attached metadata tags, gather model outputs via pre-generated files or built-in model helpers (calling APIs like Gemini or Claude, or hosting custom local models), and pass responses to an LLM judge (e.g., Gemini) or pre-loaded human evaluations.
- **Mitigating Judge Biases**: LLM Comparator implements two core features to eliminate evaluation bias:
  1. `flip_position`: Randomizes response presentation order to counteract LLM position bias (where judges systematically favor the first response).
  2. Multiple Judges / Ensembles: Configurable judge counts to run multiple trials for robust scoring.
- **Rationales and Clustering**: The pipeline processes verbose judge explanations into concise bullet points, then executes a clustering step that semantically groups similar feedback into digestible themes to highlight why models win or lose along specific dimensions.
- **Artifact Generation**: Outputs are compiled into a standalone `comparator.json` file containing metadata (prompts, models, judge configurations), results (per-prompt data, winning model, rationale), and summary statistics. This file powers an interactive UI allowing granular inspection and acts as an archival, Git-trackable replay record.
- **Tool Ecosystem Guidance**:
  - *LM Evaluation Harness*: Standard for academic benchmarking (e.g., MMLU, HellaSwag).
  - *LLM Comparator*: Recommended for qualitative comparisons to select top candidate models.
  - *OpenAI Evals*: Tailored for OpenAI API users, production monitoring, and regression testing.
  - *Hugging Face Evaluate*: Best for calculating standardized metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore) across teams.
  - *LangChain Evaluators*: Ideal for evaluating complex multi-step chains and agents.

### Takeaways
- **Slice, Don't Average**: Global win rates mask critical domain-specific failures. Teams should use metadata tags to analyze performance across key prompt slices.
- **Calibrate LLM Judges**: Before executing massive evaluation runs, align LLM judges against 10–20 golden human-labeled prompts.
- **Judge Ensemble Best Practices**: Use an odd number of judges for tie-breaking, avoid using either candidate model (A or B) as the judge, and favor open-source/open-weight models for auditability.
- **Beyond Text**: Evaluation must expand into tool use, function-calling trajectories, CI/CD automated testing, red teaming/safety, and multimodal models spanning audio and imagery.

talks.teaser: Details architecting the AI Bridge: Integrating LLMs and DMN With Drools, Sp... Tim Wuthenow & Alex Porcelli and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Tim Wuthenow and Alex Porcelli present a hybrid AI architecture that combines Large Language Models (LLMs) with Symbolic AI to overcome the limitations of each approach. Using a healthcare scenario—a patient with stage 4 cancer on a remote island with no hospital beds available—they illustrate why LLMs alone are insufficient: these models provide statistically correct but situationally inappropriate answers because they lack deterministic, context-aware decision logic tailored to specific business requirements.

## Key Topics
The speakers argue that while LLMs excel at processing unstructured data and complex inputs, they are inherently non-deterministic and trained on static data. Conversely, Symbolic AI—specifically through Decision Model and Notation (DMN) and the Drools rule engine—provides deterministic, auditable, and business-friendly decision-making. The solution is a hybrid bridge that leverages both technologies via the MCP (Model Context Protocol).

## Technical Details
**DMN (Decision Model and Notation):** An open standard that is graphically visualizable, human-readable, and executable. Decisions are modeled using decision tables (similar to spreadsheets with conditions and outcomes). DMN is non-developer-friendly, allowing business analysts and domain experts to define and modify rules. It is self-documented and LLMs are already trained to explain DMN logic.

**Drools:** An open-source rule engine maintained by the Apache Foundation that processes DMN models. It has been used for approximately 20 years.

**MCP Integration:** A Spring Boot application serves as an MCP server that exposes a catalog of available DMN decisions, along with their input and output schemas. This enables LLMs to discover, query, and execute decisions dynamically through a bidirectional interaction layer.

**Implementation:** A straightforward Spring Boot Maven project with DMN files in the resources folder and Drools as a dependency. The system provides REST endpoints, Java APIs, and native APIs alongside the MCP interface. In the demo, they illustrated querying available policies, understanding input requirements (e.g., "Is patient a cancer patient?", "Hospital beds available?"), executing decisions, and dynamically adding new rules (e.g., stroke-patient routing) without recompiling application code.

## Takeaways
- **Hybrid AI is Essential:** Combining statistical (LLM) and deterministic (Symbolic AI) models produces robust, auditable, and contextually appropriate decisions.
- **Auditability and Compliance:** DMN's deterministic nature and traceability are critical for regulated industries (healthcare, finance, insurance) where decisions must be replayed and explained to regulators.
- **Instant Adaptation:** Changes to DMN rules are immediately available to LLMs through the MCP protocol, enabling real-time policy updates (e.g., Friday evening pricing changes).
- **Business Ownership of Rules:** Domain experts can modify business logic without developer intervention, accelerating decision-making cycles.
- **Open Standards Matter:** DMN's status as an open standard ensures vendor independence and LLM familiarity.

talks.title: Open Source Tools To Empower Ethical and Robust AI Systems
talks.teaser: Examines open Source Tools To Empower Ethical and Robust AI Systems and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented by Alberto Rodriguez and Miguel Fontana (crediting Vicente, who co-developed the initial talk delivered at KubeCon), this session surveys the landscape of open-source tools and frameworks designed to secure artificial intelligence systems across their lifecycle. As generative AI and large language models (LLMs) transition from experimental pilots to production applications, organizations face amplified risks ranging from prompt injection to unintended database deletion or unauthorized script execution. The speakers argue that open-source tools are vital for independent verification, democratizing safety access, and preventing "evaluation gaming" where model creators are the sole evaluators.

### Key Topics
The speakers structure AI security tooling into three core categories across the software development life cycle (SDLC):
- **Pre-deployment / Evaluation Tools:** Assessing models during training and prior to deployment using red teaming, benchmark suites, and probe-based evaluation.
- **Runtime Tools:** Intercepting interactions during live inference via input/output filters, guardrails, and real-time monitoring.
- **Knowledge and Governance Frameworks:** Industry guidance, threat taxonomies, and operational adoption roadmaps.

### Technical Details
The presentation details several open-source tools, data sets, and frameworks:
- **Runtime Guardrails & Filters:**
  - *LLM Guard (Protect AI):* A runtime Python library that filters inputs and outputs against jailbreaks and injections. Notably, it detects and obfuscates PII (e.g., emails) before dispatching requests to inference providers, restoring original data upon response receipt (noting this can impact streaming responses).
  - *Guardrails AI:* Provides an open-source hub of reusable input/output validators (supporting custom Python validators or judge models such as Llama Guard) to block or monitor risky outputs.
- **Pre-deployment & Evaluation Engines:**
  - *Garak (Nvidia):* A probe-based vulnerability scanner for LLMs that runs repeated test prompts and detectors to identify toxic output or policy failures across non-deterministic responses.
  - *Promptfoo:* An evaluation and red-teaming tool focused on model comparison and custom metrics/datasets with graphical reporting.
  - *Giskard:* Scans models for hallucinations, bias, and prompt injection, and includes the RAG Evaluation Toolkit (RAGET) to generate targeted test suites for retrieval-augmented generation applications.
- **Toolkits and Specialized Models:**
  - *Purple Llama (Meta):* Includes *Llama Guard* (input/output moderation model evaluating 13 MLCommons hazard categories plus code interpreter abuse), *Prompt Guard* (detects prompt injections and jailbreaks), and *Code Shield* (a static analysis library inspecting assistant code generation).
  - *Adversarial Robustness Toolbox (IBM / Linux Foundation):* Evaluates traditional machine learning classifiers against evasion/adversarial noise attacks (e.g., video classification manipulation).
  - *AI Fairness 360 (IBM / Linux Foundation):* Implements bias metrics, group/individual fairness estimators, and disparate impact detectors across the training lifecycle.
- **Governance Frameworks:**
  - *OWASP GenAI Security Project:* Evolves the LLM Top 10 into governance checklists, red-teaming intelligence, and an AI security solutions landscape catalog.
  - *FINOS AI Governance Framework (Linux Foundation):* Caters to financial institutions with detailed risk catalogs and mitigation strategies.

### Takeaways
The speakers observe that while dependency deprecation and data set rot remain practical challenges, the open-source AI security ecosystem is maturing rapidly with active corporate backing and community contributions. Engineers can now mix and match open-source tools to secure the entire SDLC—from pre-deployment red teaming to runtime guardrailing—enabling organizations to look beyond vendor system cards and independently verify AI safety.

talks.title: Mind the Gap - A Developer's Roadmap To Building AI Agents
talks.teaser: Demonstrates mind the Gap - A Developers Roadmap To Building AI Agents and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Ivan Pedrazas from Docker shares practical lessons, architectural decisions, and tooling developments from Docker's journey in building AI agents. The session traces the evolution from early efforts like the GenAI stack and Docker's internal agent 'Gordon' to contemporary frameworks such as Agentic Compose, Docker Agent Builder, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations. Pedrazas highlights how building agents differs fundamentally from standard software development due to non-deterministic behavior, context constraints, and the shifting dynamics of tool execution and local security.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of AI Tooling at Docker**: Tracing Docker's path from analyzing poorly maintained Dockerfiles on GitHub to announcing the GenAI stack, developing the Gordon agent, launching Docker Model Runner, and supporting multi-framework setups via Agentic Compose.
- **Agents vs. Workflows**: Distinguishing between deterministic workflows (or rules engines) and autonomous agents powered by LLMs that make independent runtime decisions.
- **Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Tool Budgeting**: How MCP connects LLMs to external tools and services, the role of an MCP Gateway/registry, and the criticality of managing 'tool budgets' to prevent exhausting context window limits.
- **Testing and Error Handling in Agentic Systems**: Rethinking unit and integration testing when interacting with non-deterministic agents, including how tools handle initialization failures and errors.
- **Agent Security and Local Secrets Management**: Why standard local development security assumptions fall short when agents run third-party MCP servers loaded with sensitive API keys, and Docker's approach to process-isolated secret injection.

### Technical Details
- **Agentic Compose and Agent Frameworks**: Docker introduced Agentic Compose to orchestrate agents alongside models, tools, secrets, and volumes in Compose files. It provides reference architectures (such as the Sock Shop demo) across frameworks including CrewAI, Agno, and A2A. Tooling has progressed toward Docker Agent Builder and running agent CLI tasks via 'cagent' and 'dagent'.
- **Non-Deterministic Error Recovery in MCP**: Traditional APIs fail early on missing configurations. Pedrazas demonstrates that MCP servers should instead connect and expose tools even with invalid configurations. This allows the LLM to inspect errors and proactively invoke self-healing or setup tools (e.g., executing a Docker command to spin up and initialize a local Couchbase database on behalf of the user).
- **MCP Gateway**: Acts as an API gateway/ingress between the agent and various MCP servers, providing a centralized boundary to apply policies, manage interceptors, and ensure agents call tools securely.
- **Local Secret Isolation**: While developers historically tolerated plaintext secrets on local workstations, running multiple MCP servers with third-party tokens (e.g., Notion, Google) demands stronger boundaries. Docker introduced container labels and local secret definitions (e.g., via `local mcp secrets`) where secrets are injected as files. Only the specific container process can read the secret file; inspection via `docker debug`, `docker exec`, or lateral access from another container results in 'permission denied'.

### Takeaways
- **Adaptability Over Sunk Costs**: Rapid iteration in AI requires developers to be willing to drop tools and frameworks they spent months building if better paradigms emerge.
- **Design for Agent Consumption**: Build MCP tools recognizing that the caller is an autonomous, non-deterministic agent rather than a human or rigid API client; error messages should empower the agent to self-correct.
- **Security Cannot Be Deferred**: The introduction of autonomous agents with access to broad tooling necessitates robust gateway interception and strictly bounded secrets management even within local developer environments.

talks.title: Open Source for ESIM Integration - Harald Welte, sysmocom GmbH
talks.teaser: Evaluates open Source for ESIM Integration - Harald Welte, sysmocom GmbH and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Harald Welte of sysmocom GmbH discusses the technical landscape and practical implementation of eSIM technology for embedded devices using open-source software. The talk demystifies cellular smart card terminology, traces the evolution from classic 2G SIM cards to USIMs and virtualized eSIMs (eUICC), evaluates existing GSMA standards across consumer, M2M, and IoT segments, and demonstrates how open-source tooling such as `lpac` can be used to manage eSIM profiles on embedded systems.

### Key Topics
- **Terminology and Architecture**: Clarifying the distinction between SIM (2G), USIM (3G/4G/5G logical application), and eSIM/eUICC (Embedded Universal Integrated Circuit Card). An eSIM profile is conceptually a cryptographically secured and signed container (analogous to a file system archive with metadata and optional Java Cardlets) downloaded onto an eUICC chip.
- **eSIM Architectures (M2M vs. Consumer vs. IoT)**: The original M2M specification (SGP.01/02) used centralized remote control without an LPA, but failed to deliver smooth operator switching and required high minimum order volumes. Consumer eSIM (SGP.22) uses a decentralized pull model managed by a Local Profile Assistant (LPA) communicating with a Subscription Manager Data Preparation+ (SMDP+) server. The emerging IoT specification (SGP.31/32) bridges these models by splitting LPA duties between the on-device IPA and a centralized eSIM IoT Remote Manager (eIM), allowing standard consumer profiles to be managed centrally.
- **Open Source LPA Implementation (`lpac`)**: While operating a production SMDP+ server requires onerous and costly GSMA Security Accreditation Scheme (SAS) certifications, the client-side LPA requires no accreditation. Welte details `lpac`, an open-source C-based client that interfaces with SMDP+ over HTTP and communicates with the eUICC using APDU drivers.
- **Modem and Chip Interfacing**: Discusses how embedded Linux devices communicate with soldered (e.g., MFF2) or removable plastic eUICCs. Communication occurs across cellular modems using either 3GPP TS 27.007 AT commands (`AT+CCHO`, `AT+CCHC`, `AT+CGLA`) to manage logical channels and APDUs, or Qualcomm's QMI UIM subsystem.
- **Testing and Verification**: Under GSMA SGP.26, developers can utilize test certificates with a publicly disclosed root CA to conduct thousands of profile download and management tests without incurring commercial operator subscription costs.

### Technical Details
- **Cryptographic Binding**: Profiles downloaded from an SMDP+ are encrypted specifically for the target eUICC's public key (derived from a GSMA PKI). Once profile binding occurs, that profile cannot be installed on another eUICC.
- **Notifications and State Verification**: Actions such as enabling, disabling, and deleting profiles generate cryptographically signed notifications inside the eUICC, which the LPA retrieves and uploads back to the SMDP+ to prove state changes.
- **Form Factors & Hardware**: eUICCs share identical electrical and logical transmission layers with classic smart cards and can be deployed in standard removable plastic formats or surface-mount packages (e.g., standard form factor MFF2).
- **Multiple Enabled Profiles (MEP)**: While version 2 eUICC specifications restrict devices to a single enabled profile at a time, version 3 introduces MEP, enabling a single eUICC to support dual concurrent network registrations over a multiplexed UART bus to the modem.

### Takeaways
- Embedded developers can retrofit or design eSIM-capable devices using open-source LPA clients like `lpac` without proprietary client software vendor lock-in.
- The consumer eSIM ecosystem currently offers the broadest availability at unit quantities of one, while SGP.32 IoT specifications and open-source eIM tooling will enable centralized fleet management using consumer profiles.
- Developers testing eSIM integrations should leverage SGP.26 test certificate infrastructure to eliminate commercial recurring costs during development.

talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented by Dhruva (Texas Instruments) and Kevin (BayLibre), this presentation explores the complexities of CPU power management on ARM64 SoCs, focusing specifically on debugging CPUIdle and suspend-to-idle (S2Idle) states. While the fundamental goal of CPUIdle is to save power by idling when no tasks are running, achieving deep idle states involves complex interactions across Linux device trees, kernel frameworks, and ARM Trusted Firmware (TF-A) executing at elevated privilege levels (EL3).

### Key Topics
- **Linux CPUIdle and Suspend-to-Idle:** Understanding the role of the scheduler, CPUIdle drivers, and governors in selecting idle states based on predicted sleep duration versus waking latency. Unlike suspend-to-RAM, suspend-to-idle freezes user space, suspends drivers, and keeps IRQs enabled without CPU hotplugging, allowing CPUIdle to select the deepest available state.
- **Power State Coordination Interface (PSCI):** The standardized ARM specification governing power management calls between EL1 (Linux) and EL3 (TF-A), including platform-coordinated versus OS-initiated modes and parameter validation.
- **Device Tree Configuration:** How idle states, bit-encoded PSCI suspend parameters (both original and extended formats), and state hierarchies (core, cluster, system) are exposed to the kernel.
- **Timekeeping Dependencies:** The role of architected ARM timers, clock sources, and clock events in power management transitions.

### Technical Details & Case Studies
- **Case Study 1: Missing Device Tree Idle States & Firmware Panics:** On an upstream BeaglePlay board running mainline Linux and Buildroot, suspend-to-idle failed because no idle states were defined in the device tree. The CPUIdle driver failed to probe, defaulting to the architecture-specific `WFI` instruction without calling `tick_freeze`, leaving timers and softIRQs active. After adding idle states to the device tree, the firmware panicked because the PSCI suspend parameter was unrecognized. The issue was resolved by implementing the `validate_power_state` callback in TF-A to map the parameter to a platform retention state.
- **Case Study 2: Silent CPUIdle Rejection Due to Local Timers:** When configuring deeper power-down states with the `arm,psci-suspend-param` and `local-timer-stop` flag, the CPU local architected timers are powered down. Linux silently refused to select the state because no alternative wakeup timer existed. The fix required extending an upstream driver for an always-on domain timer to register clock source and clock event providers, enabling Linux to switch to a broadcast timer before entering deep idle.
- **Case Study 3: The System Fails to Wake:** In suspend-to-idle on an SoC with a separated main domain and always-on domain, a low-power co-processor (e.g., Cortex-M4 or R5) and timer woke the SoC and prompted TF-A to restore the main domain. However, because no hardware interrupt reached ARM's Generic Interrupt Controller (GIC), Linux saw no pending wakeup event and immediately instructed TF-A to go back to sleep. Fixing this required ensuring an interrupt was properly routed to the GIC to trigger CPUIdle's resume logic.
- **Debugging Strategies:** Standard JTAG debugging often disconnects when CPU power domains shut down or inadvertently prevents idle entry because debug stepping acts as an interrupt. Traditional `printk` fails when serial consoles power down. Recommended alternatives include toggling GPIOs monitored with a logic analyzer, using `trace_printk`, and capturing Ftrace traces using `trace-cmd`, Kernel Shark, or Perfetto.

### Takeaways
Debugging ARM64 low-power states requires close coordination between Linux kernel drivers, device trees, and vendor-specific firmware hooks in ARM Trusted Firmware. Developers must ensure alternative always-on broadcast timers are registered when local timers stop, correctly encode PSCI parameters according to ARM specs, and ensure wakeup events trigger GIC interrupts. Future improvements include enhancing idle state tracing in visualization tools and enabling shared trace buffers between firmware and kernel spaces.

talks.title: Extending BCC as a Data Source for System Monitoring
talks.teaser: Outlines extending BCC as a Data Source for System Monitoring and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, an engineer from LG Electronics introduces an approach and patch to extend the BPF Compiler Collection (BCC) as an automated data source for modern system monitoring and diagnostic pipelines. While BCC contains a rich collection of battle-tested, production-ready eBPF tools that offer deep kernel and user space visibility with low overhead, these tools were historically designed for standalone human consumption via the console. This presentation details how BCC tools can output standardized, structured time-series metrics directly without sacrificing BCC's standalone identity.

### Key Topics
- **Limitations of Standalone BCC Tools**: Tools like `biolatpct`/`biotop` print human-readable text tables. When updated, text formats frequently change and include non-standard noise like startup banners, making string parsing fragile and resource-heavy for automated pipelines.
- **Modern Monitoring Ecosystem Integration**: Modern pipelines collect structured metrics (measurements, labels, values, timestamps) into time-series databases for anomaly detection and graphing. Traditional tools lacked a direct, standard bridge to feed these systems.
- **Design Principles for Metric Output**:
  1. *Preserving Standalone Nature*: Keep existing human-friendly output intact by default while adding separate command-line options for structured metric emission.
  2. *Minimizing Overhead*: Implement direct structured output within BCC rather than relying on external string-scraping wrappers that consume excess CPU and break easily.
  3. *Protocol Extensibility*: Decouple the metric extraction interface from wire protocols (e.g., InfluxDB Line Protocol), allowing eBPF experts and monitoring system developers to contribute independently.
  4. *Testability and CI Verification*: Implement automated CI tests using standardized protocol specifications to verify structured outputs without requiring external database dependencies.

### Technical Details
- **Architecture**: eBPF tools typically consist of an in-kernel program storing data into eBPF maps and a user space program reading and displaying that data. The patch enhances the user space formatting layer.
- **Supported Protocols and Examples**: Line protocol was chosen as an initial industry-standard format compatible with time-series databases. Examples were shown comparing the default console table of tools like `biotop` and `syscount` against their formatted line protocol output.
- **Unified Diagnostic Dashboards**: By streaming structured data from multiple BCC tools (`biotop`, `syscount`, and a memory reclamation tool) into a time-series database, metrics were visualized simultaneously. This enables tracking I/O spikes, correlating anomalies across subsystems, and establishing baselines for automated or AI-assisted pattern analysis.

### Takeaways
- Directly integrating structured metric export inside BCC bridges the gap between low-level eBPF tracing and modern observability backends.
- The patch currently supports three BCC tools, with a roadmap to expand across more diagnostic and tracing tools.
- Decoupled metric and protocol interfaces make it easy for contributors to add new protocol serializers without needing deep eBPF kernel expertise.

talks.title: Defense in Depth: High Speed Cloud Native With Soft- and H... Ralph Squillace & Ben De St Paer-Gotch
talks.teaser: Outlines defense in Depth: High Speed Cloud Native With Soft- and H... Ralph Squillace & Ben De St Paer-Gotch and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented by Ben De St Paer-Gotch (GitHub) and Ralph Squillace (Azure Core Upstream), this presentation explores how WebAssembly (Wasm) components and microVM technologies like CNCF Hyperlight can revolutionize developer automation and security. Addressing the limitations of traditional container packaging for lightweight, ephemeral workloads, the speakers demonstrate practical methods to isolate, distribute, and execute automation tasks with millisecond-level cold starts. They also examine how compiling modular Wasm tools enables deterministic execution and fine-grained policy enforcement for AI agents and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.

### Key Topics
- **Limitations of Container Sandboxing for Small Automations**: Containers were designed for long-running processes rather than isolated, per-request function invocations. They introduce container and VM boundary overhead, multi-arch build friction, image bloat, and cold starts measured in seconds.
- **WebAssembly Components & Per-Request Ephemerality**: WebAssembly operates as an open standard (W3C) offering strong mathematical software isolation, cross-platform portability, and instantaneous memory reclamation per invocation without persistent state bleed.
- **Porting Node.js Frameworks (Probot) to Wasm**: Compiling existing JavaScript/Node tooling (such as GitHub app framework Probot) into Wasm components using tools like `componentize-js`, packaging them into OCI registries (such as GHCR via `wackage`), and running them on constrained edge hardware.
- **Hardware-Enforced Defense in Depth via Hyperlight**: The CNCF Hyperlight project embeds microVM technology directly beneath functions/Wasm runtimes, delivering sub-millisecond to 2-millisecond boot times without OS or distro overhead.
- **Deterministic Tooling for AI and LLMs with Waset**: Taming non-deterministic LLMs and AI coding assistants by providing dynamic, sandboxed, policy-enforced Wasm components as structured tools for MCP servers.

### Technical Details
- **Probot to Wasm Pipeline**: A standard Probot application targeting GitHub webhooks was bundled and compiled into a WebAssembly component using `componentize-js`. Despite bundling an embedded JavaScript engine, application code, and Node compatibility shims, the resulting uncompressed, debuggable component was only 51 MB—far smaller than a full Node container image. The component was distributed via GitHub Container Registry (GHCR) as an OCI artifact using `wackage` and executed across differing architectures (including an edge Particle.io device with 5G connectivity) using `wasmtime` and SMEI tunneling.
- **Hyperlight MicroVM Benchmarks**: Running Hyperlight microVMs demonstrated cold execution per request and pooled warm executions (using a pool of 50 microVMs sized at ≤8 MB each with dedicated vCPUs). Across Windows/WSL networking, execution latencies measured roughly 1 to 2 milliseconds per request, dropping into sub-millisecond execution on bare metal.
- **Waset MCP Tool Foundry**: Using Microsoft's open-source `waset` project, tools for LLM agents are defined as immutable, standalone Wasm components rather than unrestricted local bash scripts or full CLI installations. An LLM (GitHub Copilot) was guided by an extensive, expert-authored specification to autonomously author, build, and troubleshoot a GitHub issues triage tool in Wasm. The runtime environment dynamically loads the component and requires explicit user consent/policy checks before granting access to network and system resources.

### Takeaways
- WebAssembly components provide a secure, ephemeral execution model where state is destroyed after each request, avoiding cross-call contamination.
- Pairing Wasm software sandboxing with Hyperlight microVMs provides hardware-level defense in depth at microsecond to millisecond latency.
- Rather than exposing broad command-line permissions to LLMs, developers can build 'foundries' that supply deterministic, scoped, and policy-governed Wasm tools for AI agent workflows.

talks.title: Power Dynamics, Rug Pulls, and Other Corporate Impacts on OSS Sustainability
talks.teaser: Investigates power Dynamics, Rug Pulls, and Other Corporate Impacts on OSS Sustainability and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Open source software ecosystems increasingly reflect complex power dynamics reminiscent of historical feudalism. Large cloud service providers frequently monetize open source software without contributing back proportionately, placing financial strain on the smaller companies maintaining those codebases. In response to investor and board pressure to capture revenue, several single-vendor projects have executed "rug pulls" by shifting from open source licenses to restrictive non-open source licenses. While these shifts temporarily flip power away from cloud providers, they disenfranchise outside contributors and users. In turn, affected communities and cloud providers often respond through rebellious collective action by initiating hard forks. This presentation examines the dynamics, data, and outcomes of several prominent relicensing events and their forks, providing practical guidance for evaluating open source sustainability and mitigating disruption risk.

### Key Topics
- **Feudal Power Imbalances in OSS**: Cloud providers dominate usage and monetization, while commercial project stewards, outside contributors, and users navigate shifting leverage points.
- **Mechanisms of Rug Pulls**: Relicensing under non-OSI licenses (e.g., SSPL, Elastic License) or shifting binaries, packages, and development behind closed doors (e.g., Perforce's actions with Puppet; Linkerd stable artifacts; Bitnami container images).
- **Hard Forks as Rebellious Collective Action**: Unlike GitHub social forks used for standard contributions via pull requests, hard forks establish competing development lines (e.g., OpenSearch from Elasticsearch, OpenTofu from Terraform, and Valkey from Redis).
- **Impact on Contribution and Governance**: How contributor diversity, foundation stewardship (Linux Foundation, CNCF, Apache Software Foundation, Eclipse), and contributor agreements dictate post-fork viability.

### Technical Details
Using empirical research from the CHAOSS Data Science Initiative stored in Jupyter notebooks, the speaker examined contribution patterns (commits, additions, deletions, lines of code, and corporate affiliations) across primary project repositories:
- **Elasticsearch to OpenSearch**: In the year before and periods after Elasticsearch relicensed to SSPL/Elastic License, Elastic employees accounted for 95%–97% of code additions and deletions, with at most three non-Elastic contributors making 10 or more commits annually. Adding AGPLv3 later did not attract significant non-employee contributors. Amazon's fork, OpenSearch, was initially dominated by internal Amazon developers before gradually shifting toward broader outside participation and moving to the Linux Foundation.
- **Terraform to OpenTofu**: Prior to relicensing, HashiCorp employees made nearly all significant commits. Following relicensing, OpenTofu was established immediately under the Linux Foundation. Significant contributions came from companies like Spacelift, with developers learning the codebase rather than having migrated from the upstream core team.
- **Redis to Valkey**: Unlike Elasticsearch and Terraform, Redis had a robust external contributor base prior to relicensing (e.g., contributors from Amazon, Alibaba, Tencent, Huawei, Ericsson). Following relicensing, external contributors ceased contributing five or more commits to Redis. In Valkey's first year under the Linux Foundation, 52 people across 13 companies contributed, 22 of whom were historical Redis contributors.
- **Usage Proxies**: Drawing on research linking GitHub stars and forks to project usage, relicensed projects experienced temporary spikes in forks (as users saved code snapshots) followed by permanently reduced trajectory in new stars and forks. While hard forks saw post-announcement spikes, both originals and forks currently coexist in parallel, though foundation-backed forks show stronger community traction.

### Takeaways
To minimize vulnerability to rug pulls and project abandonment, organizations and maintainers should heed specific indicators:
- **Avoid Contributor License Agreements (CLAs)**: CLAs consolidate relicensing authority within a single corporate entity. Developer Certificates of Origin (DCOs) protect against unilateral license changes.
- **Prioritize Neutral Foundations and Governance**: Projects governed by neutral foundations (Linux Foundation, CNCF, ASF) foster level playing fields. However, neutral ownership alone is insufficient if development is monopolized by a single firm (as shown when Grafana forked Cortex to create Mimir under AGPLv3).
- **Evaluate Contributor Diversity and Viability**: Rely on metrics models such as CHAOSS Project Viability Models and CHAOSS Practitioner Guides to assess organizational distribution, responsiveness, and contributor sustainability. Active corporate participation and contributing upstream remain the most effective defenses against unilateral rug pulls.

talks.title: Sponsored Session: Who Do the Robots Work For? The Surprisingly Simple Answer to AI's... Dave Lockie
talks.teaser: Details sponsored Session: Who Do the Robots Work For? The Surprisingly Simple Answer to AIs... Dave Lockie and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
# Overview
In this talk, Dave Lockie, a strategy wrangler at Automattic, addresses AI alignment and modern technological development from a human and embodied perspective. Prompted by Tim Berners-Lee's question, "Who does the AI work for?", Lockie explores how AI systems and robots reflect the values, states, and intentions of those who create them. He argues that technological alignment is not solely a technical problem solvable through nonprofits, open source, or blockchain consensus mechanisms, but is deeply intertwined with human emotional states, burnout, and embodied cognition.

# Key Topics
- **The Alignment Question:** Lockie discusses how robots and AI embody different values depending on their creators—ranging from commercial vacuum cleaners to autonomous vehicles and Buddhist temple robots. He points out that AI proliferates widely and is trained on collective human digital exhaust.
- **Limitations of Conventional Tech Solutions:** In seeking alignment mechanisms, Lockie examined nonprofits (referencing OpenAI's shift toward corporate structures), open-source software (which can also be used maliciously and suffers from maintainer burnout), and crypto/Web3 systems (noting Bitcoin's consensus is narrowly focused on ledger states rather than complex human values).
- **The Hyper Ego and Cognitive Overload:** Lockie describes how immersive screen use disconnects people from physical reality, trapping them in rational mental loops driven by the personal super-ego. When connected across global digital networks, this aggregates into what he terms the "hyper ego"—a disembodied, reactive collective intelligence that AI models ingest and mirror.
- **Embodied Intelligence and the Gibbons:** Citing an interview by James Bridle, Lockie shares an evolutionary biology study on tool use among primates. While other great apes easily used tools on the ground to retrieve food, gibbons failed until tools were hung overhead. Because gibbons brachiate in the tree canopy, their intelligence is embodied and adapted to upward movement. Lockie uses this to demonstrate that intelligence cannot be separated from physical embodiment and environmental context.

# Technical Details
- **Audience Slido Experiment:** Lockie conducted an interactive experiment using Slido to test word association tasks under two physiological states: first while overstimulated and distracted by phones/notifications (leading to fragmented, scattered responses), and second after guided triangle breathing (inhale 3s, exhale 3s, hold empty 3s), illustrating how collective performance and coherence change with biological state.
- **Information Networks (Truth vs. Order):** Referencing Yuval Noah Harari's book *Nexus*, Lockie highlights the tension in information networks between generating truth versus producing order and power, noting corporate AI models often prioritize predictable profits, order, and engagement over wisdom and human well-being.
- **Reframing Techniques:** Drawing inspiration from Laurie Voss (creator of npm), Lockie suggests cognitive reframings—such as viewing AI as "additional intelligence" rather than "artificial intelligence," and reframing problems as puzzles.

# Takeaways
- **"Robots Work for Whoever Builds Them":** The ultimate answer to who robots work for is simple: they serve the creators who build them. The true challenge lies in deciding who we want to be and what values we bring while building these systems.
- **Embodied Self-Regulation:** Tech workers and open-source maintainers facing burnout should integrate practices to drop out of purely rational overdrive and reconnect with their bodies (e.g., triangle breathing, movement, breaks).
- **Inefficiency as a Feature:** Embracing deliberate slowness, nuance, and space for human connection prevents systems from encoding tyranny and prioritizing speed and efficiency over humanity.

talks.teaser: Examines sponsored Session: From Fear to Framework: How Open Source Enables Safe Citizen Develo... Nicky Pike and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Nikki Pike, Field CTO for Coder, presents a perspective on AI-assisted "vibe coding" and citizen development by drawing direct parallels to the do-it-yourself (DIY) home improvement industry. Rather than framing AI development through either extreme—fearing it will eliminate all software engineering jobs or dismissing it as dangerous and unviable—Pike argues that AI serves as a powerful middle ground. Much like consumer power tools enable homeowners to perform maintenance without replacing licensed contractors, AI empowers non-technical departmental employees to solve internal problems while highlighting the continued necessity of professional software architects.

### Key Topics
- **The DIY Construction Analogy**: The talk compares citizen coding to the DIY home improvement market. DIY tools, instructional media (like YouTube and HGTV), and peer review communities do not replace licensed contractors; rather, they handle smaller projects and help customers articulate better requirements to professionals.
- **Open Source Principles in Citizen Development**: Safe citizen development relies on core open-source software (OSS) principles: transparency (openly inspecting code), community review (peer and IT oversight), and shared knowledge (standardizing on common languages and architectures).
- **Enterprise Governance vs. Shadow IT**: When enterprises ignore demand for AI tools, employees resort to "Shadow IT"—pasting sensitive intellectual property into public AI tools or running unmanaged scripts locally. Providing managed workspaces curbs this risk.
- **The Evolving Role of Engineers**: Software engineers are shifting from manual code typists to architectural leaders and reviewers. Pike emphasizes that AI functions like an inexperienced junior developer or an advanced interactive tutorial, requiring human oversight, verification, and boundary setting.

### Technical Details
- **Workspace Isolation and Guardrails**: Using centralized developer workspace platforms like Coder, organizations can isolate citizen developers from production environments. Sandboxed Git repositories and dedicated environments prevent unauthorized access to customer-facing code bases and live databases.
- **Failure Containment and Ephemeral Environments**: In unmanaged environments, AI hallucinations or recursive loops can alter or inject tens of thousands of unwanted lines into a codebase. Containerized or remote workspaces allow teams to discard broken environments instantly without spending days unwinding local corruptions.
- **Distinguishing Low-Code/No-Code from AI**: Low-code and no-code graphical tools rely on rigid, predetermined logic structures and often introduce vendor lock-in. AI development models draw from vast training corpuses across diverse languages (e.g., Java, Go, Python), allowing plain-language prototyping that fits directly into standard source code repositories.
- **Target Use Cases**: Appropriate applications for enterprise citizen development include internal campaign ROI dashboards, workflow automations, and departmental data visualizations. Critical applications, production data modifications, and customer-facing interfaces remain strictly restricted to qualified software engineering teams.

### Takeaways
- Citizen development in the enterprise is an economic inevitability; organizations must build governance and guardrails rather than attempting total prohibition.
- Open-source principles—transparency, community review, and shared knowledge—provide the foundational framework for safe AI adoption.
- Organizations should adopt a "ceiling fan" approach: start citizen developers on bounded, low-risk internal utilities rather than enterprise-critical systems.
- AI acts as an accelerator for documentation, boilerplate code, and exploratory wireframing, enabling professional engineers to focus on architectural integrity, security, and performance.

talks.title: BASIL - What's New, What's Next
talks.teaser: Investigates BASIL - Whats New, Whats Next and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
# Overview
In this talk, Luigi Pelleia, Principal Software Quality Engineer at Red Hat and member of the ELISA Technical Steering Committee, presents BASIL, an open-source tool hosted under the ELISA Linux Foundation project. BASIL was originally developed at Red Hat to manage work items and build traceability matrices for ISO 26262 functional safety compliance certification for Red Hat In-Vehicle Operating System (Automotive Linux / rivals). The tool connects software specifications, manuals, or source code (split into snippets) with requirements, test specifications, test cases, and justification records.

# Key Topics
- **Traceability Matrix Management**: BASIL maps hierarchical relationships between source code or specification snippets, software requirements, test specifications, test cases, and justification notes, calculating completeness and showing gaps in a waterfall view.
- **Embedded and External Test Integration**: Incorporates Red Hat's TMT (Test Management Tool) as an embedded engine to run test suites across containers, VMs, or physical hardware via SSH. It also interfaces with external test frameworks including Linaro LAVA, GitLab CI, GitHub Actions, KernelCI, and Testing Farm.
- **Recent Enhancements**: Addition of a deployment script managing Podman containers and volumes, improved user management (usernames, email configuration for password resets, granular permissions, permission cloning across components), browser independence away from Chrome-specific APIs, and requirement/test case importing.
- **In-App AI Assistance**: Integration with OpenAI-compatible endpoints (demonstrated using Ramalama) to automatically generate draft test specifications and test cases from reference documentation.
- **SPDX Safety SBOMs**: Generation of SPDX-based Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) in JSON format capturing the full traceability matrix and database row checksums.

# Technical Details
BASIL exposes both a web user interface and an HTTP REST API, with a backend written in Flask (tested via pytest) and frontend end-to-end testing running in Cypress. Requirements can be imported from CSV, YAML, JSON, spreadsheets, StrictDoc, and SPDX JSON formats. Test cases can be scanned and imported from remote Git repositories adhering to the TMT format, such as Fedora Glibc or kernel test repos.

The tool supports external execution triggers and result parsing; during the demo, Pelleia demonstrated connecting to a local LAVA instance using preset YAML configurations, triggering a test run, viewing status and logs, and linking external test results back into the BASIL traceability matrix. Additionally, test execution parameters and scenarios can be adjusted dynamically through environment variables or TMT context variables.

# Takeaways
BASIL provides an open-source, automated solution for safety-critical traceability and evidence collection. The roadmap includes:
- Supporting the evolving SPDX Safety Profile (targeting version 3.1), which is also utilized by continuous compliance tools like InfoMagnus.
- Project baselining directly inside the tool to capture point-in-time certification snapshots.
- Migrating backend storage from SQLite to PostgreSQL to handle concurrent users, multiple workers, and multithreading.
- Enhancing file management (nested folders) and expanding LAVA integration to support Jinja templating.

talks.summary:
## Overview
Amit Pund from Linaro presents the challenges and recent developments in maintaining Android Open Source Project (AOSP) on development boards, using the metaphor of "bootloops and coffee" to describe the daily reality of AOSP developers. The talk covers major features landing in AOSP, integration of external projects, and community initiatives emerging in response to recent policy changes by Google.

## Key Topics

### Generic Bootloader Library (GBL)
Android suffers from bootloader fragmentation because each vendor implements their own bootloader rather than using a common standard. GBL is an EFI application developed and distributed by Google that provides a standardized, vendor-agnostic bootloader interface. It abstracts underlying platform-specific implementations, reducing the need for vendors to rework bootloaders with every Android release. However, vendors must implement custom EFI protocols to use GBL—it is not a simple drop-in replacement.

### Page Size Agnostic AOSP Builds
ASP has been refactored to support both 4K and 16K page sizes without requiring separate builds. 16K page size builds deliver 5–10% performance improvements at a cost of 9% additional memory. Implementation required removing page size assumptions, using 16K-aligned binaries, and employing separate loadable segments. File system configuration varies by platform: F2FS offers best performance when block size matches kernel page size, while ext4 and EROFS support agnostic builds with 4K block sizes.

### System Core Changes and Notable Additions
Recent system core updates simplified booting AOSP from external storage (e.g., USB drives) by introducing a kernel command line argument to locate boot devices via partition UUID. Notably, UUID parsing is case-sensitive and requires lowercase formatting. Android also enabled more aggressive asynchronous kernel module probing and introduced ashmem compatibility patches to support legacy applications expecting ashmem IOCTLS on the upstream MEMFD driver.

### Common Development Breakages
Amit identifies recurring integration challenges: HID-to-AIDL framework transitions requiring device manifest updates; build configuration tool changes (such as restrictions on external Android.mk files); aggressive movement toward Bazel builds; and GKI-related failures including symbol list modifications, protected kernel module restrictions, and kernel config changes affecting vendor drivers.

### External Projects: Kernel and Graphics
Integrating the Linux kernel upstream and Mesa/Freedeno graphics involves ongoing friction: device tree nodes and configuration files lack stability guarantees and are frequently renamed; LSM policies cause difficulties with peripheral device probing; upstream developers may resist Android-specific bug reports without reproducibility on standard distributions; and firmware-related bugs often go unfixed due to vendor disinterest in legacy devices. Mesa/Freedeno integration introduces build breakages from cross-platform changes and incomplete support for certain GPU features.

### Major AOSP Policy Shifts
Two significant policy changes affect the community: AOSP main branch entered read-only mode in March 2025, with development moving to the new "Android latest release" branch. Changes submitted to this branch require cherry-picking by Google into internal builds before appearing in quarterly releases—with no notification mechanism for external developers confirming acceptance. Additionally, Google removed Pixel device configurations that had historically served as reference platforms for undocumented AOSP hooks, leaving custom ROM developers without official build targets and forcing reliance on virtual devices like Cuttlefish.

### Community Initiatives
In response to these challenges, the Devboards for Android and AOSP devs projects provide umbrella spaces for system developer collaboration. Devboards for Android offers reference boards, pre-built images, and a staging area for pending AOSP patches using AOSP-style code review workflows. These initiatives aim to bridge the gap left by Google's policy changes and foster development of generic AOSP features across multiple platforms and SoCs.

## Takeaways
Keeping pace with AOSP requires managing constant updates across the OS core, external projects, and tooling. Community-driven initiatives are essential as official Pixel device support has contracted. Upstream-first development brings long-term benefits but involves friction with kernel maintainers and fragmentation across vendors. The shift to a read-only AOSP main branch and reduced Pixel reference support represent significant changes to the AOSP development ecosystem, making collaborative, community-led projects increasingly vital for device maintainers and custom ROM developers.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Oscar (also known as Andreas) discusses the challenges of open-source license compliance and Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) automation. Treating open-source compliance simply as running an automated scan fails because static analysis cannot capture technical nuances, runtime interactions, customer usage, or dynamic conditions across complex software like Chromium or FFmpeg. Oscar argues that while scanners provide baseline data, human interpretation and scalable automated workflows are essential, introducing an agentic multi-agent approach to handle SBOM assessment and enrichment alongside emerging security concerns in AI models.

### Key Topics
- **Limits of Traditional Scanners**: Static scans struggle with complex licensing obligations (such as copyleft boundaries, patent covenants, dynamic vs. static linking, and language-specific behaviors like Python under LGPLv3). Scanners also often operate as black boxes or produce errors that persist for years.
- **SBOM Practicalities and Pitfalls**: In real-world environments processing hundreds of thousands of packages, SBOMs act primarily as transfer protocols rather than guarantees of data quality. They frequently suffer from missing hashes, incomplete assertions, proprietary identifier notations, and cross-format parser incompatibilities (e.g., SPDX, CycloneDX).
- **Agentic Automation Architecture**: To augment open-source engineers, Oscar details a multi-agent system comprising reflex, utility, and goal-based agents. The system ingests SBOMs, extracts package identifiers, queries enrichment APIs, and generates legal notices and scorecard assessments.
- **Open Source and Local Agent Frameworks**: Demonstrating live via an n8n workflow and an offline open-source agentic platform running in Docker, Oscar shows how local or cloud-hosted models (such as OpenAI models, Gemini, Amazon Bedrock, and Claude) can automate compliance tasks.
- **Emerging AI Model Compliance & Security Risks**: Reviewing research across 160,000 AI models, Oscar highlights a severe lack of licensing and provenance declarations, coupled with security threats such as backdoors, obfuscated pickle files, cryptominers, and models phoning home.

### Technical Details
- **Multi-Agent Pipeline**: In the demonstrated pipeline, incoming emails with SBOM JSON attachments trigger a parsing workflow. A reflex agent extracts package identifiers; a utility agent queries external data providers (including ClearlyDefined, VulnerableCode, Scorecard, and ScanCode.io) to resolve provenance and vulnerability data; and a goal-based agent synthesizes the results to draft tentative legal notices.
- **Community Data Feeds**: External resources such as ClearlyDefined, VulnerableCode, Debricked/deps.dev, Software Heritage, and ScanCode provide geoprovenance for export control, database tracking, and scan results without over-relying on single-vendor commercial scanners.
- **AI Model Vulnerabilities & Statistics**: 
  - Of 160,000 evaluated AI models, only 35% carried declared licenses, 14% had provenance/dataset declarations, and 18% declared bias.
  - Around 700 models were improperly registered inside other packages under purported permissive licenses.
  - Historical and ongoing security attacks include the 2020 `torch-triton` supply chain issue, 2023 PoisonGPT backdoors, JFrog's 2024 discovery of over 100 malicious models, the 2024 YOLOv8 cryptomining ingestion, and 2025 obfuscated pickle backdoors.
  - Serialized `.pickle` files and binary blobs frequently evade standard Software Composition Analysis (SCA) tools because tools do not inspect or parse serialized model layers unless dynamically executed.

### Takeaways
- **Agents Augment, Not Replace**: AI agents act as copilots for compliance engineers by remembering past decisions and managing high ticket volumes, but human engineers must remain the final authority on risk decisions.
- **Need for Dynamic & Runtime SBOMs**: Static ingestion scans miss runtime threats, particularly binary payloads embedded inside wheels or serialized model weights. Organizations must assess open source and AI models across ingestion, build, and deployment runtime stages.
- **Expanding Compliance to AI**: Compliance programs must rapidly adapt to inspect AI models for data provenance, licensing fidelity, and malicious serialized payloads, establishing dedicated registries and inspection mechanisms.

talks.title: Bring the Power of Wireshark To Syscalls and Logs With Stratoshark
talks.teaser: Reviews bring the Power of Wireshark To Syscalls and Logs With Stratoshark and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Gerald Combs, creator of Wireshark and co-creator of Stratoshark, presented how Wireshark's proven dissection engine—which supports 3,000 protocols and 265,000 fields—can be applied to system calls and log messages. Wireshark's core strength is its ability to provide granular detail about every field in data, enabling users to build complex filters, colorize events, and graph trends. Combs drew a parallel between system calls and network packets: both form a boundary layer characterizing system behavior and revealing security or performance issues.

## Key Topics

The technical foundation rests on two libraries: **libscap** (library for system capture), which hooks into the Linux kernel via kernel module or eBPF probe to capture syscalls, and **libs** (library for system inspection), which enriches that data by mapping file descriptors to file paths, user IDs to usernames, and similar contextual information. Two main tools consume these libraries: **Cydig**, a command-line utility producing a "fire hose" of syscall output, and **Falco**, a host-based IDS that continuously monitors syscalls against rules.

**Stratoshark** is Combs's implementation: it ports Wireshark's dissection engine and UI to syscalls and logs. The tool mirrors Wireshark's layout with event-based fields (event name, process ID, username, etc.), supports Lua post-dissectors, enables filtering and stream-following, and displays rich detail for each event. Stratoshark ships with plugins for cloud audit sources—AWS CloudTrail, Google Cloud audit logs, Kubernetes audit logs—allowing forensic analysis of cloud activity.

## Technical Details

In a live demo, Combs captured remote Linux syscalls via SSH, filtered for specific processes (bash, curl), and investigated a compromised script attempting to exfiltrate `/etc/passwd`. He demonstrated filtering on file descriptor type and name, following pipe streams, and pivoting investigation by process ID. Stratoshark integrates Wireshark's ELF dissector, revealing executable format metadata within syscall captures—demonstrating Wireshark's ability to dissect non-protocol data (JPEG, PNG, MP3). A second demo showed loading an AWS CloudTrail JSON log and inspecting failed S3 bucket operations via pretty-printed JSON view.

The I/O buffer size is configurable (default 80 bytes, configurable via settings like the 512-byte snapshot limit shown). Remote capture uses SSH to run cydig under sudo, necessary for enriched privilege and process information from `/proc`. The scap file format is based on pcapng, enabling potential future mixing of syscalls, logs, and network packets.

## Roadmap and Status

Stratoshark is available as installers for Windows and macOS; Linux requires building from source. Combs noted that traditional Linux distribution packages are not yet available. The tool captures syscalls locally on Linux and remotely via SSH from any platform. Future capabilities under consideration include Windows syscall capture via Event Tracing for Windows (ETW), macOS syscall support (framework exists but unfamiliar to Combs), and integration of strace and Process Monitor file formats.

Stratoshark and Falco are separate tools sharing libscap and libs; Falco is lightweight for continuous monitoring, Stratoshark is feature-rich for forensic investigation. Version 0.9.x releases are ongoing, with version 1.0 targeted for late summer or early fall, synchronized with the next major Wireshark release. Stratoshark and Falco share similar filtering languages (not identical to Wireshark display filters), and an experimental feature converts Wireshark display filters to Falco rules.

talks.title: The Life of a Kernel Bugfix
talks.teaser: Analyzes the Life of a Kernel Bugfix and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Overview

This talk explains how to properly develop and distribute kernel bugfixes from upstream mainline through stable releases to end-user distributions. The speaker targets hardware vendors, distribution maintainers, and contractors maintaining kernel code, emphasizing an upstream-first philosophy to maximize scalability and reduce maintenance burden.

## Key Topics

**Linux Kernel Release Process**: The kernel follows a structured cycle starting with a 2-week merge window after each release, followed by 7–8 release candidates (RC) before the next stable version. Specific versions (6.6, 6.1, 6.12) are designated as long-term stable (LTS) releases, which continue receiving backported fixes from newer mainline versions.

**Distribution Kernel Categories**: Four types exist: (1) pristine upstream kernels with only binary/config differences, (2) upstream kernels with small patches for security or unapproved fixes, (3) kernels with significant downstream patches requiring merges rather than simple rebasing, and (4) kernels with extensive subsystem backports mixing code from multiple upstream versions.

**Distribution Policies**: Each distribution has different acceptance criteria: bug reports or CVE numbers, test cases/reproducers, multiple internal reviews, and varying maintenance windows. These policies differ significantly between Debian, Ubuntu, Red Hat, and others, making direct patching of all distributions non-scalable.

## Technical Details

**Mainline and Stable Process**: Contributors submit patches to subsystem maintainers for review. Patches submitted during the 2-week merge window are typically held until after RC1. Stable maintainers (Greg, Sasha) automatically cherry-pick bug fixes from mainline if tagged with `CC: stable@vger.kernel.org` or containing a Fixes tag. These are queued, tested by community volunteers, released weekly, and eventually picked up by distributions.

**Best Practices**:
- Include a Fixes tag pointing to the commit that introduced the bug
- Add `CC: stable@vger.kernel.org` to signal stable maintainers
- Include clear bug description, stack traces, and reproducers
- Keep patches small and self-contained
- Run `scripts/checkpatch.pl` for code compliance
- Send to appropriate subsystem maintainers

**Backporting Challenges**: When automatic cherry-picking fails (due to code changes), manual backports require: annotating with upstream commit references, adding sign-offs, and explaining conflicts with a scissors separator (---). This applies to patches that don't meet upstream stable policy but fit distribution policy.

**Stable Kernel Requirements**: Fixes must address bugs (crashes, hangs, data corruption), not features or trivial changes. Since February 2024, all commits in upstream releases receive CVE assignments.

## Takeaways

The optimal path is: fix → mainline → upstream stable → distributions. This scales because upstream stable has fewer requirements than individual distributions. When a fix includes a Fixes tag and stable CC, it flows automatically through the entire pipeline.

For distribution-specific issues, direct submission requires following each distribution's documented process—labor-intensive but sometimes necessary. Features face significantly higher barriers than bug fixes; the upstream-first approach is recommended for practical maintenance.

talks.title: Lightning Talk: Streaming and Processing Edge Vision Data in Real Time
talks.teaser: Demonstrates lightning Talk: Streaming and Processing Edge Vision Data in Real Time and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
# Overview
Joyce, head of developer relations for Viam (an open-source platform for building physical AI), discusses why computer vision pipelines that work perfectly in controlled environments fail at the edge and presents three design patterns for optimizing edge vision workloads without streaming data to the cloud.

# Key Topics
Joyce identifies core obstacles: CV pipelines are slow, expensive to run, and demand substantial compute and bandwidth—challenges magnified in real-world edge deployments. Vision Language Models (VLMs), while impressive, are particularly problematic for real-time actuation; even models designed for local execution like Moonbeam can take several seconds to respond.

Rather than solve problems by deploying larger models, Joyce advocates optimization through three design patterns:

**1. Continuous Local Inference**
Run models locally and send only events or metadata upstream. She demonstrates this with retail shelf monitoring: instead of streaming video to headquarters, a lightweight YOLO model runs locally to detect when shelves need restocking. The system sends only event signals when items run low, triggering either local actuation (like a light) or system-wide alerts. Frigate is cited as an open-source example running YOLO for person detection, integrable with Home Assistant, and capable of running completely offline without cloud connectivity.

**2. Sensor Fusion**
Use inexpensive sensors as low-power watchdogs to trigger compute-intensive CV operations on demand. Joyce illustrates this with whale protection: environmental sensors detect when a boat enters certain zones or reaches speed thresholds, triggering the camera and model only when needed. This reduces compute costs and false positives while working reliably on spotty satellite internet.

**3. Edge-First Systems**
Systems designed to function entirely offline. Joyce's bathroom queue example (QuickQ app at stadiums) runs fully locally on mobile devices, displaying wait times peer-to-peer without cloud dependency. Cloud sync is optional and deferred for non-time-sensitive analytics only.

# Technical Details
Across all examples, the stack centers on YOLO running on TensorFlow Lite—optimized for single-board computers and lightweight enough for local execution. Hardware acceleration options include Raspberry Pi AI hats or Coral TPU modules. Data transport uses gRPC for fast typed API calls and WebRTC for low-latency peer-to-peer communication. Viam handles orchestration and integration of models, sensors, and actuators.

# Takeaways
• Optimize down, not up: event-driven architectures and lightweight models accomplish more with less at the edge
• Send only events and metadata upstream, not raw video
• Enable offline operation for remote locations and unreliable connectivity
• Use open standards to scale from Raspberry Pi to industrial fleets
• Combine sensor data with CV to improve accuracy and reduce false positives
